explanations.explanation: That's him. The text says one of the Pharisees, "an expert in the law," tested Jesus with a question (Matthew 22:35). I bet a man like that walked up feeling ready. He brought a test to the Teacher, and friend, that is a BOLD move.

Close, since he's a religious leader, but that's not what the text calls him. Matthew 22:35 says he's one of the Pharisees, "an expert in the law." The text gives him no priest title at all. Sometimes the answer is just in the verse, and this one is sitting right there.

I can see why you'd pick it, but the verse doesn't say that. It says one of the Pharisees, "an expert in the law," steps up and tests Jesus (Matthew 22:35). No synagogue is mentioned anywhere in this moment. Stick with the title the text actually gives him.

Yes! Jesus says, "Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind." Then He adds, "This is the first and greatest commandment." The man asked for the greatest, and Jesus doesn't even hesitate. I love a straight answer.

That's a real commandment, one of the ones God gave Israel in Exodus 20:8. But it's not the one Jesus picks here. In Matthew 22:37-38, He says to love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul and mind, and calls that the first and greatest. Good commandment, wrong spot on the podium.

Honoring your father and mother is a real commandment too (Exodus 20:12). It's just not the one Jesus names as first and greatest. He says, "Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind." Then He tells the man, "This is the first and greatest commandment."

All. Jesus says to love the Lord your God "with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind." Notice He says "all" three times. That's no leftovers and no halfway, and I'm still working on my own batch of that.

Not part. Jesus says love the Lord your God "with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind." He doesn't mention a part anywhere in there. When the text says "all" three times in one line, nobody gets to keep a piece in the pocket.

"Most" sounds generous, but it's not the word Jesus uses. He says to love the Lord your God "with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind." That's all of the heart, all of the soul and all of the mind. Most of a cookie is still not a whole cookie, friend.

That's the one! Jesus says, "And the second is like it: 'Love your neighbor as yourself.'" He says it's like the first, so these two belong together. The man asked for one commandment and got a pair. Not bad for one question!

Lying to your neighbor is something the Law speaks to. It says not to bear false witness against your neighbor (Exodus 20:16). But that's not the second commandment Jesus gives here. He says, "Love your neighbor as yourself."

explanations.answer: Give to your neighbor in need
explanations.explanation: Giving to a neighbor sounds like it fits, and I bet it does. But those aren't the words Jesus uses. In Matthew 22:39, He says the second commandment is, "Love your neighbor as yourself." He doesn't spell out the how in this verse.

Not quite, and Jesus says the opposite. He says, "All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments." That means the rest of the Law hangs on them. Nothing in that sentence makes them small.
False, and you're right. Jesus says, "All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments." That's the whole Law and the Prophets hanging on them. These two are not small at all.

David it is. Jesus asks whose son the Christ is, and the Pharisees answer, "David's." David was Israel's king, and in a moment Jesus brings up what David said in the Spirit. Keep that answer in your pocket, because Jesus is about to use it.

Moses, Israel's leader, is a big name (Exodus 3:10), but he's not who they say. When Jesus asks whose son the Christ is, the Pharisees answer, "David's." That's David, Israel's king. The answer comes up again in the next question, so remember it.
Aaron was Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), but he's not the answer here. The Pharisees say the Christ is "David's" son. David was Israel's king. That's the name Jesus builds His next question on.

Right. Jesus asks, "How then does David in the Spirit call Him 'Lord'?" The "Him" is the Christ, the one they just said is David's son. David says, "The Lord said to my Lord," so he's calling that person his Lord. That's why the question lands so hard.

Saul was a king of Israel (1 Samuel 15:1), but he's not who Jesus is talking about. Jesus asks how David "in the Spirit" calls "Him" Lord, and "Him" is the Christ from the question just before. Saul isn't in this conversation at all.

Samuel was a prophet of the LORD (1 Samuel 3:20), but he isn't in this moment. Jesus asks, "How then does David in the Spirit call Him 'Lord'?" The "Him" is the Christ, the one the Pharisees just called David's son.

explanations.answer: David would be calling his own son Lord
explanations.explanation: That's the puzzle. The Pharisees say the Christ is David's son, and then David calls Him "Lord." Jesus asks, "So if David calls Him 'Lord,' how can He be David's son?" A king calling his own son Lord is a head-scratcher, and I think that's why nobody has an answer.

explanations.answer: David would be calling an enemy his Lord
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but the enemies in the verse are a different group. The line says, "until I put Your enemies under Your feet." Those are the enemies of the one David calls Lord. The puzzle is that the Pharisees said the Christ is David's son, and David still calls Him Lord.

explanations.answer: David would be calling a stranger his Lord
explanations.explanation: A stranger isn't the problem here. The Pharisees already said the Christ is David's son, so this is family. The trouble is that David calls Him "Lord" anyway. That's why Jesus asks, "How can He be David's son?"

True. The text says, "No one was able to answer a word." Not a short answer, not a mumble. These were the same Pharisees who gathered to question Jesus, and now they've got nothing. I'd have gone looking for a snack.
That's the opposite of what the text says. Matthew 22:46 says, "No one was able to answer a word." Nobody gave a reply at all. The Pharisees had plenty of questions, and not one answer.
Yes. The text says, "from that day on no one dared to question Him any further." The questions in the temple stop right there. This is the last of the questions in this group of passages.

The verse doesn't say anything about following Jesus through the city. It says, "from that day on no one dared to question Him any further." What stopped was the questioning. Read the end of the verse closely, friend.

Teaching in the temple courts isn't what the verse mentions. Matthew 22:46 says, "from that day on no one dared to question Him any further." That means no more questions for Jesus. The text doesn't say anything about teaching.
